meta: A wall-mounted radar watches posture in the room: if someone who was standing ends up on the floor and doesn't get up, it alerts the family, even in the dark or in steam, without filming anyone's face.

muc.title: Grandparents living alone
muc.text: Grandparents live alone, and the family wants to know right away if they fall, but nobody wants a camera in the bathroom. Radar sees movement without filming anyone's face.

muc.title: Detecting falls
muc.text: A wall-mounted radar device tracks the posture of people in the room. When someone who was standing suddenly ends up lying on the floor and doesn't get up, it alerts the family, even in the dark or in steam.

muc.title: Counting breaths without touch
muc.text: Radar can even count breaths, because the chest rising and falling by a few millimeters is enough to clearly change a 5 mm wave bouncing back. The channel simulated one minute of noisy signal, and the device still counted exactly 15 breaths.

muc.title: Cameras that assist endoscopy
muc.text: In hospitals, since 2021 the US has approved AI cameras that assist with colonoscopies, drawing a green box around possible polyps. The final decision still belongs to the doctor.

muc.title: Four questions to pick an eye
muc.text: The series ends with four questions. Need to read color and text? Choose a camera. Need speed in rain and darkness? Choose radar. Need a very precise distance? Choose LiDAR. Could a mistake hurt someone? Combine two or more kinds.

muc.title: See just enough
muc.text: One more principle, see just enough: in private spaces, prefer radar and process the data on the device itself.

muc.title: Ask AI to pick a sensor
muc.text: Describe your own problem to a chatbot, such as counting customers entering a shop, and ask it to compare the three eyes using these four questions. A sample prompt is in the pinned comment.
